reference.source: Stiehm's Immune Deficiencies / Nathan and Oski's Hematology of Infancy and Childhood
clinicalPearls: A rare congenital neutrophil disorder in which neutrophils (and often eosinophils) fail to produce secondary (specific) and tertiary granules together with their antimicrobial contents

Classically caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in CEBPE, encoding the myeloid transcription factor CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein epsilon; variants in SMARCD2 produce a closely related phenotype
The blood film characteristically shows neutrophils with bilobed or hypolobated nuclei resembling the Pelger-Huet anomaly and strikingly agranular cytoplasm

Patients suffer recurrent, often severe pyogenic infections of skin, ears, lungs and lymph nodes, commonly with Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas and enteric organisms, and may develop deep abscesses
Functional defects include impaired chemotaxis, disordered receptor up-regulation and reduced bactericidal activity, compounded by absence of defensins, lactoferrin and other granule proteins
Demonstrating markedly reduced or absent specific-granule proteins such as lactoferrin, alongside the typical morphology, supports the diagnosis pending genetic confirmation
Management centres on aggressive treatment and prophylaxis of infection, with haematopoietic stem cell transplantation considered in severe cases
reference.pathophysiology: CEBPE encodes a transcription factor essential for terminal neutrophil maturation and for driving expression of secondary and tertiary granule proteins. Biallelic loss-of-function abolishes production of specific granules (containing lactoferrin, transcobalamin and collagenase) and gelatinase granules together with their antimicrobial peptides, notably defensins, while also disturbing nuclear segmentation to give the bilobed morphology. The resulting neutrophils show defective chemotaxis, impaired mobilisation of surface receptors and reduced bactericidal capacity, predisposing to recurrent bacterial infection. SMARCD2, a subunit of the BAF chromatin-remodelling complex, acts in concert with CEBPE during granulopoiesis, so its deficiency yields an overlapping disorder.
additionalDifferentials: Glycogen storage disease type Ib with neutrophil dysfunction
additionalInvestigations: Peripheral blood film for bilobed, hypogranular neutrophils (pseudo-Pelger-Huet appearance)
Assays of neutrophil granule proteins such as lactoferrin and defensins demonstrating deficiency
Neutrophil functional studies including chemotaxis and bactericidal assays
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine to assess granulopoiesis
Flow cytometry or immunofluorescence for specific-granule proteins
Targeted infection work-up with imaging of suspected deep abscesses
redFlags: Recurrent deep-seated abscesses or invasive bacterial infection
Sepsis in a child with the characteristic agranular blood film
Faltering growth with chronic suppurative infection
Progressive pulmonary infection or evolving bronchiectasis
reference.prognosis: With vigilant antimicrobial treatment and prophylaxis many patients survive into adulthood, although recurrent severe infections cause considerable morbidity; haematopoietic stem cell transplantation may be curative in selected severe cases.
pitfalls: Mistaking the bilobed hypogranular neutrophils for acquired myelodysplasia rather than a congenital defect
Attributing recurrent infection to a commoner immunodeficiency without inspecting granule morphology
Overlooking the diagnosis because neutrophil counts are typically normal
Failing to separate it from myeloperoxidase deficiency or chronic granulomatous disease by functional testing
Delaying genetic confirmation and appropriate family counselling
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology of Infancy and Childhood
management: Prompt, aggressive antibiotic treatment of bacterial infections, guided by culture and covering Staphylococcus aureus and Gram-negative organisms
Long-term antibacterial prophylaxis such as co-trimoxazole to reduce recurrent pyogenic infection
Surgical drainage of deep abscesses when they develop
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation as the potentially curative option in severe disease
Regular surveillance for new infections with a low threshold for imaging and early intervention
Refer to clinical immunology and haematology and confirm the diagnosis with CEBPE and SMARCD2 genetic testing
Genetic counselling and family screening for this autosomal recessive disorder
